title: Black and White Dog, Head Turned to the Left
medium: Graphite, heightened with white chalk, orange chalk, on brown paper

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Walter C. Baker, 1964
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A drawing on brown paper of a black and white dog with its head turned to the left, made with graphite and chalk.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, public-domain flag, credit line, tags (Dogs), classification (Drawings) and image URLs read from the record

context: A drawing by the French artist Jean-Baptiste Huet, dated 1794–95, made with graphite and white and orange chalk on brown paper. Huet was well known for drawing animals, and his designs were also used for printed textiles in France.

descriptions.k: This is a drawing of a dog. The dog is black and white. It turns its head to the left. The paper is brown. Where do you see white chalk? What do you think the dog sees?
descriptions.g12: Jean-Baptiste Huet drew this dog in France long ago. He used pencil and chalk on brown paper. The dog is black and white and turns its head to the left. The brown paper shows through and helps the dog look soft. What is the dog looking at?
descriptions.g35: Jean-Baptiste Huet was a French artist who specialized in drawing animals. Here he studied a black and white dog turning its head to the left, using graphite, white chalk, and orange chalk on brown paper. The paper acts as a middle color. Look for where he used white chalk for bright spots. What does the dog's pose tell you about its mood?
descriptions.g68: Huet made this drawing in 1794–95, using graphite, white chalk, and orange chalk on brown paper. The brown ground gives a middle tone, so white chalk can show light and graphite can show dark. Huet was known for animal studies and also designed patterns for printed cloth. Notice how the dog's turned head creates a sense of attention. How does close study of one animal make it feel alive?
descriptions.g910: In this study, Huet uses graphite, white chalk, and orange chalk on brown paper to describe a dog with its head turned to the left. The toned ground sets a middle value, allowing small touches of white to read as light and graphite to describe darker fur. Studies like this show how artists trained their eyes and hands, and Huet's animal drawings also served his design work. How does the economy of the medium shape the dog's presence?
descriptions.g1112: Huet's dog study of 1794–95 shows the pleasures and discipline of drawing from observation. The toned paper, the interplay of graphite, white chalk, and orange chalk, and the arrested turn of the head produce a sense of living attention with minimal means. As Huet also supplied designs for printed textiles, the drawing raises questions about the relation between close study and decorative production, and about how an apparently modest animal study can sustain serious looking.

teacherNote.context: Jean-Baptiste Huet was a French artist known for animal drawings and for designs used on printed textiles. This 1794–95 study of a dog uses graphite and chalks on brown paper.
directions: Give students brown paper, pencil, and white chalk to draw a pet or stuffed animal.
Ask students to explain how the paper color helps the drawing and what would change on white paper.
Discuss the difference between a study and a finished artwork.
